title: Mineral Nutrition
description: Grade 11 Biology: essential mineral elements in plants, macro- and micronutrients, their roles and deficiency symptoms, and biological nitrogen fixation.

topics.title: Essential Elements: Macronutrients and Micronutrients
topics.concept:
Besides carbon, hydrogen and oxygen (which come from air and water), plants need a number of mineral elements that they absorb from the soil as ions. An element is called essential if the plant cannot complete its life cycle without it, it has a specific role that no other element can replace, and it is directly involved in the plant's metabolism. Scientists discovered these requirements using hydroponics — growing plants in a nutrient solution rather than soil — and leaving out one element at a time to see the effect.

Essential elements are grouped by the amount needed:

  • Macronutrients — needed in large amounts. These are carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and sulphur.
  • Micronutrients (trace elements) — needed in very small amounts. These include iron, manganese, copper, zinc, boron, molybdenum and chlorine.

By function, the elements act as: components of biomolecules and structures (e.g. nitrogen in proteins, magnesium in chlorophyll), activators or inhibitors of enzymes (e.g. magnesium, zinc), and regulators of the osmotic balance of cells (e.g. potassium). Even though micronutrients are needed in tiny amounts, they are just as essential — a shortage of any one causes problems.

examples.problem: Example 1: State the three criteria for an element to be called 'essential'.
examples.solution:
Recall the definition.

  • The plant cannot complete its life cycle without it.
  • It has a specific, irreplaceable role and is directly involved in metabolism.
examples.answer: It is needed to complete the life cycle, has a specific irreplaceable role, and is directly involved in metabolism.

examples.problem: Example 2: Classify nitrogen and iron as macro- or micronutrients.
examples.solution:
Sort by quantity required.

  • Nitrogen — needed in large amounts — macronutrient.
  • Iron — needed in trace amounts — micronutrient.
examples.answer: Nitrogen is a macronutrient; iron is a micronutrient.

examples.problem: Example 3: What technique is used to study which minerals are essential for plants?
examples.solution:
Plants are grown without soil.

  • Hydroponics — growing plants in a defined nutrient solution.
  • One element is left out at a time to observe the effect.
examples.answer: Hydroponics (soil-less culture), omitting one element at a time.

recap:
• Essential element: needed to complete the life cycle, irreplaceable specific role, directly in metabolism.
  • Studied by hydroponics (soil-less culture).
  • Macronutrients (large amounts): N, P, K, Ca, Mg, S (+ C, H, O).
  • Micronutrients (trace): Fe, Mn, Cu, Zn, B, Mo, Cl.
  • Roles: structure, enzyme activation, osmotic balance.

quiz.q: Nutrients required by plants in very small (trace) amounts are called:
quiz.explanation: Micronutrients (e.g. iron, zinc) are needed only in trace amounts.

quiz.q: The soil-less technique used to study mineral needs is:
quiz.explanation: Hydroponics grows plants in a defined nutrient solution.

topics.title: Roles of Minerals and Deficiency Symptoms
topics.concept:
Each essential element has particular jobs, and its shortage produces a characteristic deficiency symptom. Knowing the symptom helps farmers diagnose what a crop is lacking. Some important examples:

  • Nitrogen (N) — a part of proteins, nucleic acids, chlorophyll and many vitamins. Deficiency causes chlorosis (yellowing of leaves) and stunted growth.
  • Phosphorus (P) — part of DNA, RNA, ATP and membranes. Deficiency causes poor root growth and dark/purplish leaves.
  • Potassium (K) — helps open and close stomata, activates enzymes and maintains osmotic balance. Deficiency causes scorched, curled leaf margins.
  • Magnesium (Mg) — the central atom of the chlorophyll molecule and an enzyme activator. Deficiency causes chlorosis between the veins.
  • Iron (Fe) — needed to make chlorophyll (though not part of it) and in respiration. Deficiency causes chlorosis of young leaves.
  • Calcium (Ca) — needed for the cell wall (middle lamella) and cell division. Deficiency affects growing tips.

An important pattern: symptoms of mobile elements (like N, P, K, Mg) appear first in the older leaves, because the plant moves these elements out of old leaves to the growing young parts. Symptoms of immobile elements (like Ca, Fe) appear first in the young leaves. The most common visible symptom overall is chlorosis — the loss of green colour caused by reduced chlorophyll.

examples.problem: Example 1: Why does nitrogen deficiency cause yellowing (chlorosis) of leaves?
examples.solution:
Link nitrogen to the green pigment.

  • Nitrogen is part of chlorophyll.
  • Without enough nitrogen, less chlorophyll forms, so leaves turn yellow.
examples.answer: Nitrogen is needed to make chlorophyll; a shortage reduces chlorophyll, so the leaves yellow (chlorosis).

examples.problem: Example 2: Which element is the central atom of chlorophyll?
examples.solution:
Recall the chlorophyll structure.

  • Magnesium sits at the centre of the chlorophyll molecule.

examples.problem: Example 3: Deficiency symptoms of mobile elements like nitrogen appear first in which leaves, and why?
examples.solution:
Mobile elements are redistributed.

  • They appear first in the older leaves.
  • The plant moves these elements from old leaves to growing young parts.
examples.answer: In the older leaves, because mobile elements are moved out of old leaves to the young growing parts.

recap:
• N: proteins, nucleic acids, chlorophyll → deficiency = chlorosis, stunting.
  • P: DNA/RNA/ATP; K: stomata, osmotic balance; Mg: central atom of chlorophyll; Fe: chlorophyll synthesis; Ca: cell wall.
  • Mobile elements (N,P,K,Mg): symptoms first in old leaves; immobile (Ca,Fe): first in young leaves.
  • Most common symptom = chlorosis (loss of chlorophyll).

quiz.q: The central metal atom of the chlorophyll molecule is:
quiz.explanation: Magnesium is at the centre of the chlorophyll molecule.

quiz.q: Yellowing of leaves due to loss of chlorophyll is called:
quiz.explanation: Chlorosis is the loss of green colour from reduced chlorophyll.

topics.title: Nitrogen Metabolism and Biological Nitrogen Fixation
topics.concept:
Nitrogen is one of the most important nutrients, yet plants cannot use the abundant nitrogen gas (N₂) of the air directly. The air is about 78% nitrogen, but the two atoms are held by a very strong triple bond. Converting this unusable N₂ into a form plants can absorb (like ammonia or nitrate) is called nitrogen fixation.

Most of this is done biologically by certain microbes — this is biological nitrogen fixation, carried out by the enzyme nitrogenase. The nitrogen fixers are of two kinds:

  • Free-living fixers in the soil, such as the bacterium Azotobacter and the cyanobacterium Anabaena / Nostoc.
  • Symbiotic fixers, the most famous being Rhizobium, which lives in the root nodules of legumes (peas, beans, gram). The bacterium fixes nitrogen for the plant, and the plant supplies it with food and shelter — a true symbiosis.

Inside the plant, the fixed nitrogen (as nitrate) is first converted to ammonia and then built into amino acids and other compounds — the start of nitrogen assimilation. Because legumes enrich the soil with nitrogen through their nodules, farmers practise crop rotation, growing a legume crop to naturally restore soil fertility and reduce the need for chemical fertilisers.

examples.problem: Example 1: Why can't plants use atmospheric nitrogen (N₂) directly?
examples.solution:
Think about the nitrogen molecule.

  • N₂ has a very strong triple bond and is unreactive.
  • It must first be fixed into ammonia or nitrate before plants can use it.
examples.answer: Because N₂ is very unreactive (strong triple bond); it must first be fixed into a usable form like ammonia or nitrate.

examples.problem: Example 2: Name the bacterium that fixes nitrogen in the root nodules of legumes.
examples.solution:
Recall the symbiotic fixer.

  • Rhizobium lives in legume root nodules.

examples.problem: Example 3: How does growing legumes help improve soil fertility?
examples.solution:
Legumes host nitrogen fixers.

  • Rhizobium in their nodules fixes atmospheric nitrogen into the soil.
  • This enriches the soil with nitrogen (used in crop rotation).
examples.answer: Their root-nodule Rhizobium fixes atmospheric nitrogen, enriching the soil — the basis of crop rotation.

recap:
• Nitrogen fixation: converting unreactive N₂ into ammonia/nitrate that plants can use.
  • Biological fixation by the enzyme nitrogenase: free-living (Azotobacter, Anabaena) and symbiotic (Rhizobium in legume root nodules).
  • Fixed N → ammonia → amino acids (assimilation).
  • Legumes enrich soil → basis of crop rotation.

quiz.q: Conversion of atmospheric N₂ into a usable form is called:
quiz.explanation: Nitrogen fixation converts unreactive N₂ into ammonia/nitrate.

quiz.q: Rhizobium fixes nitrogen while living in the root nodules of:
quiz.explanation: Rhizobium lives symbiotically in the root nodules of legumes.

questions.q: Which gases/elements come from air and water, not the soil?
questions.explanation: C, H and O come from air and water; minerals come from the soil.

questions.q: An essential element is one that:
options: Can be replaced by another element
Is needed to complete the life cycle and has a specific role
questions.explanation: Essential elements are required to complete the life cycle and have specific irreplaceable roles.

questions.q: Nutrients needed in large amounts are:
questions.explanation: Macronutrients (N, P, K, etc.) are needed in large amounts.

questions.q: Which of these is a micronutrient?
questions.explanation: Zinc is a micronutrient (trace element).

questions.q: The soil-less culture method used to identify essential elements is:
questions.explanation: Hydroponics grows plants in a defined nutrient solution.

questions.q: Nitrogen is a component of all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Cellulose is a carbohydrate (no nitrogen); proteins, nucleic acids and chlorophyll contain nitrogen.

questions.q: The central atom of the chlorophyll molecule is:
questions.explanation: Magnesium sits at the centre of chlorophyll.

questions.q: General yellowing of leaves due to lack of chlorophyll is:
questions.explanation: Chlorosis is loss of green colour from reduced chlorophyll.

questions.q: Deficiency symptoms of mobile elements (N, P, K) appear first in:
questions.explanation: Mobile elements are moved from old to young leaves, so symptoms show first in older leaves.

questions.q: Calcium is mainly needed for the:
questions.explanation: Calcium is part of the cell wall (middle lamella) and is needed for cell division.

questions.q: Plants cannot use atmospheric N₂ directly because it is:
questions.explanation: The strong N≡N triple bond makes N₂ unreactive; it must be fixed first.

questions.q: The enzyme that carries out biological nitrogen fixation is:
questions.explanation: Nitrogenase fixes nitrogen in nitrogen-fixing microbes.

questions.q: Rhizobium fixes nitrogen in the root nodules of:
questions.explanation: Rhizobium lives symbiotically in legume root nodules.

questions.q: Which is a free-living nitrogen fixer?
questions.explanation: Azotobacter is a free-living soil nitrogen fixer.

questions.q: Growing legumes to enrich soil nitrogen is the basis of:
questions.explanation: Legumes restore soil nitrogen, which is why crop rotation includes them.

questions.q: A plant grown in a complete nutrient solution but with nitrogen removed shows yellow, stunted growth. This shows nitrogen is:
questions.explanation: Removing only nitrogen causes deficiency, proving it is essential with a specific role.

questions.q: Deficiency of an immobile element such as calcium shows first in young leaves because the element:
options: Cannot be moved from old leaves to new growth
Is not needed by young leaves
questions.explanation: Immobile elements stay put, so new growth runs short first.

questions.q: A farmer alternates a wheat crop with a bean (legume) crop. The main benefit is that the legume:
questions.explanation: Legume root nodules fix nitrogen, restoring fertility for the next crop.

questions.q: Although needed in tiny amounts, a micronutrient like molybdenum is still essential because:
options: Its absence still prevents normal growth/completion of the life cycle
It is not used at all
questions.explanation: Essentiality is about having a specific irreplaceable role, not the quantity needed.

questions.q: Both iron and magnesium deficiencies cause chlorosis, yet they differ because magnesium is part of chlorophyll while iron is needed to:
options: Synthesise chlorophyll (it is not part of it)
questions.explanation: Mg is a structural part of chlorophyll; Fe is needed for its synthesis but is not part of the molecule.

questions.q: In a Rhizobium–legume association, the plant benefits from fixed nitrogen and the bacterium benefits from food and shelter. This relationship is:
questions.explanation: Both partners gain, making it a mutualistic symbiosis.
